questions.q: According to Lenz's Law, what does an induced emf always give rise to?
options: A current that creates a magnetic field reinforcing the original change in flux through the circuit
A current that creates a magnetic field that opposes the original change in flux through the circuit
A current whose magnetic field opposes the existing flux, regardless of whether it is rising or falling
A current that opposes the magnet, attracting it on approach and repelling it on withdrawal
questions.explanation: Lenz's Law states that an induced emf always gives rise to a current that creates a magnetic field that opposes the original change in flux through the circuit. The key word is 'change' - when flux is falling the induced field reinforces the original field to oppose the decrease, so 'opposes the flux' and 'opposes the magnet' are both wrong phrasings.

questions.q: Why is the minus sign placed in Faraday's Law of Induction, and of what principle is Lenz's Law a consequence?
options: The minus sign sets the magnitude of the induced emf; Lenz's Law is a consequence of the conservation of charge
The minus sign reminds us of the direction of the induced emf; Lenz's Law is a consequence of the Principle of Conservation of Energy
The minus sign indicates the emf is always negative; Lenz's Law is a consequence of the conservation of momentum
The minus sign converts flux to current; Lenz's Law is a consequence of the right-hand grip rule
questions.explanation: The minus sign in Faraday's Law of Induction is placed there to remind us of the direction of the induced emf, and Lenz's Law is a consequence of the Principle of Conservation of Energy. The sign carries direction only, never magnitude, so it is discarded in any size calculation.

questions.q: The N pole of a magnet approaches a coil connected to a galvanometer. As the magnetic flux density within the coil increases, what does the induced current do, and how is its direction deduced?
options: It sets up a magnetic field that opposes the change, making the near face repel the approaching N pole; direction from the right-hand rule for coils
It sets up a magnetic field that aids the change, attracting the approaching N pole; direction from the right-hand push rule
It produces no field because a steady magnet induces nothing; direction is undefined
It sets up a field that attracts the magnet to conserve energy; direction from the left-hand rule
questions.explanation: As the magnet approaches, the magnetic flux density within the coil increases, and the induced current sets up a magnetic field that opposes this change, so the induced magnetic field of the coil repels the approaching N pole. The direction is deduced using the right-hand rule for coils: the thumb points along the induced field within the coil and the curl of the fingers gives the current.

questions.q: A metal ring lies in a uniform magnetic field directed into the page and is then removed from the field. In which direction does the induced current flow in the ring, and why?
options: Anticlockwise, to create a field out of the page that opposes the removal
Clockwise, to create a magnetic field into the page that replaces the field lines that are leaving
It alternates direction as the ring leaves the field
No current flows because removing the ring does not change the flux
questions.explanation: Initially the external field lines pass into the page through the ring; as it is removed these field lines reduce in number, so the induced current flows to create a magnetic field that replaces the missing lines. By the right-hand rule for coils this means the current flows clockwise, and it stops once the ring is entirely out of the external magnetic field.

questions.q: Faraday's Law of Induction states that the induced emf in a circuit is equal in magnitude to which quantity?
options: The total magnetic flux threading the circuit
The rate at which the magnetic flux through the circuit is changing with time
The strength of the steady magnetic field passing through the coil
The resistance of the circuit multiplied by the flux
questions.explanation: Faraday noted that the induced emf in a circuit is equal in magnitude to the rate at which the magnetic flux through the circuit is changing with time. A strong but steady field induces nothing because the flux is not changing; for a coil of n turns the emf is n times greater.

questions.q: A rectangular loop of dimensions 0.25 m by 0.3 m takes 2.0 s to fully enter a perpendicular magnetic field of strength 0.66 T. Calculate the magnitude of the induced emf.
working: \(\Delta\phi_B = 0.05\,\mathrm{Wb}\) (the initial field through the loop is zero)
questions.explanation: Find the area, then the change in flux as the loop enters the field, then apply Faraday's Law. The magnitude of the induced voltage is 0.025 V; the minus sign only indicates the induced emf opposes the change in magnetic flux.

questions.q: A flat circular coil of 50 turns and radius 0.10 m lies with its plane perpendicular to a uniform field (theta = 0). The field is steadily reduced from 0.40 T to zero in 0.20 s. Calculate the magnitude of the induced emf.
questions.explanation: Faraday gives the magnitude (about 3.1 V); the minus sign is dropped because it only carries direction. The direction is part of Lenz's Law: the flux is decreasing, so the induced current flows to oppose the decrease by reinforcing the original field direction.

questions.q: Eddy currents are an application of Lenz's Law. When a metal sheet is being removed from a magnetic field, what is true of the force on the eddy current?
options: The magnetic fields set up by the eddy currents aid the change, so the force assists the motion of the sheet
The magnetic fields set up by the eddy currents oppose the change, so the force is always opposite to the direction of motion of the sheet
The eddy currents produce no force because the sheet is not a coil
The force is always at right angles to the motion, neither helping nor hindering it
questions.explanation: Eddy currents are an application of Lenz's Law: the magnetic fields set up by the eddy currents oppose the changes in the magnetic field acting in the metal. The force on the eddy current, found with the right-hand push rule, is always opposite to the direction of motion of the sheet, so it is harder to move the metal when the field is present.

questions.q: From memory, run the proof-by-contradiction that shows the induced current must oppose the change in flux. What breaks if it instead reinforced the change?
keyPoints: Assume the induced current aids the change: e.g. the coil attracts an approaching magnet instead of repelling it.
The attraction accelerates the magnet, giving a greater rate of change of flux, which by Faraday's law induces a larger emf and current.
A larger current means a stronger field and stronger attractive force - a runaway positive-feedback loop with no brake.
Both kinetic energy (magnet) and electrical energy (coil) grow with no energy input: a perpetual motion machine, which violates conservation of energy and is impossible.
Therefore the induced current must oppose the change that produced it - this is Lenz's law.
questions.explanation: If you hit the chain - assume, accelerate, runaway feedback, perpetual motion, violation, conclude oppose - grade yourself Good or Easy. Memory spine: State, assume, run away, violate, conclude, track.

questions.q: Recall the two mnemonics from the episode: the energy pathway (where every joule of induced electrical energy comes from and goes to), and the three-step procedure for finding the induced current direction.
keyPoints: Energy pathway - Work, Watts, Warmth: you do mechanical work against the opposing force, it becomes electrical energy in the induced current, then heat in the resistance (I squared R).
Every joule of induced electrical energy is paid for by a joule of mechanical work - nothing is free.
Direction procedure - Change, Oppose, Grip: (1) how is the flux changing? (2) which induced field opposes that change? (3) right-hand grip rule to turn that field into a current.
Increasing flux: induced field points opposite the external field; decreasing flux: induced field points the same way to replace it.
questions.explanation: Work, Watts, Warmth is the energy spine of the extended response; Change, Oppose, Grip is the practical direction-finding skill. The grip (curl) rule - thumb for field, fingers for current - is not the palm rule for the force on a moving charge.

questions.q: Explain how the direction of an induced current is consistent with the law of conservation of energy. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: If an induced current reinforced the change in flux that produced it rather than opposing it, the resulting force would accelerate the source of the change - for example a magnet approaching a coil. The faster motion would increase the rate of change of flux, inducing a still larger current and a still stronger force, in a runaway feedback loop that increases both kinetic and electrical energy with no external energy input. This would be a perpetual motion machine and would violate the law of conservation of energy. Therefore the induced current must flow so as to oppose the change that produced it, which is Lenz's law. The induced electrical energy is in fact paid for by the mechanical work done against the opposing force, which becomes electrical energy and then heat.

criteria.descriptor: Sets up the contradiction: a reinforcing current accelerates the source, giving a runaway feedback loop.
Names that this would be a perpetual motion machine / energy from nothing, violating conservation of energy.
Concludes the induced current must oppose the change, and identifies mechanical work as the real energy source.

questions.explanation: The verb 'explain' on this dot-point means run the energy argument, not just state the rule. Bank the marks by naming the runaway feedback, the perpetual-motion violation, and the conclusion that the current must oppose the change.
